questions.q: Why does `parser.add_argument("prompt", help="...")` with no leading dashes make `prompt` a required argument?
options: It doesn't — all argparse arguments are optional by default
The help text is what makes it required
argparse treats an argument name without leading dashes as a required positional argument; running the script without it prints a usage message and exits automatically
It requires a separate required=True flag to work
questions.explain: In argparse, an argument name given without a leading -- or - (like "prompt") is a positional argument, which is required by default. Omit it and argparse automatically prints a usage error and exits — no extra code is needed.

questions.q: What design pattern does the `CompletionClient` class follow, and from which earlier lesson?
options: A singleton pattern from Chapter 6
The class-based client wrapper pattern from Chapter 3, Lesson 17 — configuration held in __init__, one clear method exposed
An abstract base class pattern that hasn't been covered in the course
A dataclass pattern with no methods
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly calls back to Lesson 17's class-based client wrapper: store configuration (the api_key) in __init__, and expose behavior through a clear method (ask()).

questions.q: What does `resp.raise_for_status()` do inside the `ask()` method?
options: It raises an HTTPError exception if the response's status code indicates a failure, instead of silently returning bad data
It prints the response status code to the console
It retries the request automatically
It converts the response into JSON
questions.explain: raise_for_status() checks the response's HTTP status and raises an exception for 4xx/5xx codes. This makes failures explicit and catchable immediately, rather than letting bad data flow silently into the rest of the program.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say catching specific exceptions and exiting with `sys.exit(1)` is what "separates a script from a tool"?
options: Because sys.exit(1) makes the program run faster
Because scripts cannot use try/except blocks at all
There's no real difference — it's just a style preference
Because a real tool gives the user a clear, readable error message and a non-zero exit code other programs can detect, instead of dumping a raw, confusing traceback
questions.explain: Dumping a raw traceback at a user is a hallmark of an unfinished script. Catching specific, expected failure modes and responding with a clear message plus a conventional non-zero exit code (so other programs/scripts calling this tool can detect failure) is what makes something feel like a finished, reliable tool.

questions.q: What does `unittest.mock.patch("ask.requests.post")` accomplish in the test?
options: It permanently disables requests.post for the rest of the program
It sends a real POST request to verify the API is online
It temporarily replaces requests.post with a fake object for the duration of the `with` block, so the test can run instantly without making a real network call
It deletes the requests library from the test environment
questions.explain: patch() swaps in a mock object in place of requests.post only within the with block's scope, letting the test control exactly what the "API" returns without touching the real network — making the test fast, deterministic, and independent of network availability.
